notes.h: Excretion and the kidney's two jobs
notes.b: Every cell produces waste as it carries out its chemical reactions, and some of that waste is harmful if it stays in the body. The kidneys are the main organs that clear it away, and they do a second job at the same time: keeping the body's fluids balanced.
points: Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism (the chemical reactions in cells). Faeces are not excreted: they are undigested food that was never absorbed, so passing them out is egestion.
The kidneys excrete urea, excess water, excess salts and excess hydrogen ions in urine. Other organs help: the lungs excrete carbon dioxide, and sweat removes some water, salts and a little urea.

Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids (the units of proteins) by deamination, the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of an amino acid. It is carried dissolved in the blood plasma to the kidneys.
Urea is toxic if it builds up, so it must be removed continuously rather than in occasional bursts.

Transport between environments: blood (the internal environment) carries wastes to the kidneys, the kidneys transfer them from the blood into urine, and urine is passed out of the body (the external environment).
At the same time the kidneys return useful substances (glucose, amino acids, most of the water and most of the salts) to the blood, so nutrients are not lost in the urine.
The kidneys have two roles: excretion (removing urea and other wastes), and osmoregulation and homeostasis, which regulate the volume, water content, salt concentration and pH of the body fluids.
Both roles use the same two processes: filtration of the blood (squeezing small molecules out of it), then reabsorption (taking back what the body needs). What is not reabsorbed is urine.
notes.tip: You may be asked to define excretion and to tell it apart from egestion: excretion removes metabolic waste, egestion removes undigested food. Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids, not in the kidney. The kidney only removes it.

notes.h: The kidneys and their blood supply
notes.b: The kidneys sit well protected at the back of the body and are supplied directly by a large artery. That position and supply let them filter a large volume of blood at high pressure.
points: The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs at the back of the abdomen, one on each side of the vertebral column (backbone), just below the diaphragm. The lowest ribs partly protect them.
The right kidney is slightly lower than the left because the liver lies above it and takes up space.
Each kidney is embedded in a layer of fat that cushions it against physical damage and helps hold it in place, and is covered by a tough outer membrane, the renal capsule.
The adrenal glands (small hormone-producing glands) sit on top of the kidneys.
Each kidney receives blood from a renal artery, a short wide branch of the aorta (the body's main artery), so blood arrives at high pressure and in large volume, which suits filtration.
Filtered blood leaves by the renal vein, which joins the vena cava (the large vein returning blood to the heart).

Blood in the renal vein has less urea, less oxygen and less glucose than blood in the renal artery, and more carbon dioxide because the kidney cells respire. It is the blood vessel with the lowest urea concentration in the body.

Diagram: front view of the urinary system. Label two kidneys, renal arteries from the aorta, renal veins to the vena cava, ureters, bladder, sphincter muscles and urethra. The adrenal glands on top of the kidneys may be shown.
notes.tip: A common question asks you to compare blood in the renal artery and the renal vein: the vein has less urea, oxygen and glucose, and more carbon dioxide. You may also be asked what the fat around the kidneys does: it protects them from physical damage.

notes.b: Once urine has formed it must be carried away, stored and released at a suitable moment. Three structures do this in turn: the ureters carry it, the bladder stores it and the urethra lets it out.
points: There are two ureters: narrow muscular tubes, one from the renal pelvis (the funnel-shaped collecting space inside each kidney) down to the bladder.
The ureter walls contain smooth muscle that moves urine by peristalsis (waves of contraction), so urine reaches the bladder whatever the body position, not just by gravity.
The urinary bladder is a hollow muscular bag in the lower abdomen (pelvis) that stores urine.
The bladder wall is elastic and folded, so it can stretch to hold a large volume and contract to empty.

Two rings of sphincter muscle (muscle that closes an opening) at the bladder outlet keep it closed: an inner one that works automatically (involuntary), and an outer one under conscious (voluntary) control, which young children learn to control.
The urethra is the single tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
In males the urethra is longer, runs through the penis and also carries semen. In females it is short and opens just in front of the vagina.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the ureter and the urethra, the commonest error here. There are two ureters, each carrying urine from a kidney to the bladder. There is one urethra, carrying urine from the bladder to the outside.

notes.b: Cut a kidney lengthways and you can see that it is not uniform inside. The three regions each have a different role in making and collecting urine.
points: A kidney cut lengthways shows three regions: cortex, medulla and renal pelvis.
Cortex: the dark outer layer, under the renal capsule.
Medulla: the paler inner layer, divided into cone-shaped renal pyramids.

Renal pelvis: a funnel-shaped space on the inner (concave) side that collects urine and leads into the ureter. No filtration happens in the pelvis and urine is not changed there, so it is only a collecting space.
notes.tip: You may be asked to label a kidney section (cortex, medulla or pyramid, renal pelvis, ureter). Never say that filtration or reabsorption happens in the pelvis: it only collects urine.

notes.h: Nephrons and the sites of filtration and reabsorption
notes.b: The real work of the kidney is done by microscopic tubes called nephrons. Each one first filters the blood, then takes back what the body needs, and the leftover liquid becomes urine.
points: Each kidney contains about one million nephrons, microscopic tubules that are the kidney's filtering units, so together they give a huge filtering surface. Each runs from the cortex down into the medulla and back.
The nephron tubules drain into collecting ducts that run through the pyramids and open into the renal pelvis.
Filtration takes place in the cortex: blood is forced at high pressure through knots of capillaries (glomeruli) into the cup-shaped tops of the nephrons (Bowman's capsules).

Small molecules (water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea) are filtered out of the blood. Blood cells and plasma proteins are too large, so they stay in the blood. The filtered liquid is called the filtrate.
Reabsorption (taking useful substances back into the blood) takes place in the cortex, in the coiled tubules, and in the medulla, in the loops of Henle and the collecting ducts.
All the glucose and amino acids, most of the salts and most of the water are taken back into the blood. The remaining liquid, carrying urea and excess salts and water, is urine.

Diagram: longitudinal section of a kidney. Label renal capsule, cortex, medulla, renal pyramid, renal pelvis, ureter, renal artery and renal vein. Draw one nephron from cortex into medulla to show where filtration and reabsorption happen.
notes.tip: Learn the sites: filtration in the cortex, reabsorption in the cortex and the medulla, and urine collected in the renal pelvis. You may be asked in which region filtration happens, or where named nephron parts are found.

notes.h: Urine: its contents and its volume
notes.b: Urine is what is left of the filtrate once the body has taken back what it needs. Its volume and concentration change from hour to hour, which is how the kidneys keep the water content of the blood steady.
points: Urine is mostly water, with urea, salts (mainly sodium chloride) and other wastes dissolved in it.
Healthy urine contains no protein and no glucose, because protein is not filtered out of the blood and all the glucose is reabsorbed.
After drinking a lot of water, the kidneys produce a large volume of dilute (pale) urine, which gets rid of the extra water.
When water is short (little drinking, heavy sweating in exercise or hot weather, or diarrhoea), a small volume of concentrated (dark yellow) urine is produced, so the body saves water.
The control is by the hormone ADH. There is more on this in ADH and osmoregulation; here you only need the effect on urine.
notes.tip: Expect to be asked how the volume of urine changes with water intake or sweating: more water drunk gives more, paler urine, and heavy sweating gives less, darker urine.

notes.b: Water is not the only thing the kidneys balance. They also adjust salts and acidity, and together this keeps the body's internal conditions steady.
points: Salt balance: after a salty meal the kidneys excrete more salt, and when salt is short they reabsorb more.
Keeping the salt and water concentration of the blood steady stops body cells from gaining or losing water by osmosis (the movement of water across a membrane towards the more concentrated solution).
pH: the kidneys remove excess hydrogen ions from the blood in urine, helping to keep blood pH at about 7.4. There is more on this in Minerals.
This is homeostasis: the kidneys keep the internal environment constant whatever is eaten or drunk, much as a thermostat holds a room at one temperature.

notes.h: Path of urine from kidney to urethra
notes.b: Urine is made all the time, but it is passed out only now and then. This sequence shows how it travels and why release can be delayed.
points: 1. Urine forms continuously in the nephrons and drains from the collecting ducts into the renal pelvis.
2. Peristalsis in the ureter carries it to the bladder in small spurts.
3. The bladder fills and its wall stretches. Stretch receptors in the wall send nerve impulses that give the urge to urinate.
4. To urinate, the bladder's muscular wall contracts and the sphincters relax. The outer sphincter relaxes under voluntary control, which is learned after early childhood.
5. Urine leaves the body through the urethra.
notes.tip: Learn this as an ordered sequence, and keep ureter (kidney to bladder) and urethra (bladder to outside) the right way round. You may be asked to name the tube that carries urine to the bladder.

notes.b: Each part of the urinary system has features that suit its job. Examiners ask you to link structure to function, so learn these as pairs.
points: Fat layer around each kidney: protects it from physical damage.
Renal artery branching directly from the aorta: delivers high-pressure blood for filtration.
About one million nephrons: a huge filtering surface.
Cortex full of capillary knots: the site of filtration.
Long tubules and loops in the medulla: the site of reabsorption.
Funnel-shaped renal pelvis: collects urine.
Muscular ureters: move urine to the bladder by peristalsis.
Elastic bladder with sphincters: stores urine and allows controlled release. The urethra is the exit for urine from the body.
notes.tip: The syllabus asks you to relate the structure of the urinary system to its function in filtering and removing waste. Give the feature and its function together.

notes.h: Urine testing as a health link
notes.b: Because healthy urine contains no glucose or protein, finding either one in a urine sample tells a doctor that something is wrong.
points: Glucose in urine is a sign of diabetes, because blood glucose is so high that not all of it can be reabsorbed.
Protein in urine is a sign of damage to the kidney's filters, because healthy filters do not let protein through.
Urine tests are also used to detect drugs, for example in sport.

notes.b: If the kidneys stop working, the body can no longer clear its wastes or balance its fluids. There are two treatments: a machine that does the kidney's job, or a replacement kidney.
points: If the kidneys stop working, urea, salts and water build up in the blood and the person will die without treatment.
Treatment is by dialysis or by a kidney transplant.
A transplant gives a working kidney, but the patient must take drugs to stop the immune system rejecting it, because the body treats the new kidney as foreign. There is more on this in Immunity.

notes.b: A dialysis machine copies the kidney's filtering. It uses diffusion across a membrane to clean the blood.
points: The patient's blood is pumped through a machine where it flows past a selectively permeable membrane (one that lets only some substances through), with dialysis fluid on the other side.
Urea and excess salts diffuse out of the blood into the fluid, because their concentration is higher in the blood.
The fluid contains glucose and salts at normal blood concentrations, so these are not lost from the blood. Blood cells and proteins are too large to cross the membrane.
Dialysis must be repeated several times a week, because it does not work continuously the way healthy kidneys do.

keyTerms.definition: The removal of the waste products of metabolism from the body.
A toxic nitrogen waste made in the liver from excess amino acids and removed from the blood by the kidneys.
The control of the water and salt concentration of the body fluids.
The tough outer membrane that covers each kidney.
The dark outer region of the kidney, where filtration takes place.
The paler inner region of the kidney, divided into renal pyramids, where reabsorption takes place.
The funnel-shaped space at the inner side of the kidney that collects urine and leads into the ureter.
A narrow muscular tube that carries urine from the renal pelvis of a kidney to the bladder by peristalsis.
The tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
A ring of muscle that closes an opening; the bladder has an involuntary inner sphincter and a voluntary outer sphincter.
A knot of capillaries in the cortex where blood is filtered under high pressure.
The cup-shaped top of a nephron that surrounds a glomerulus and receives the filtrate.
The liquid that is filtered out of the blood into the nephron, containing water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea but not blood cells or plasma proteins.
A treatment for kidney failure in which urea and excess salts diffuse out of the blood across a selectively permeable membrane into a dialysis fluid.

questions.prompt: Name the regions labelled A, B and C on a diagram of a kidney (cortex, medulla, renal pelvis) and state the function of the ureter.
questions.model: The cortex is the dark outer layer under the renal capsule, where filtration takes place. The medulla is the paler inner layer, divided into renal pyramids, where reabsorption takes place. The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped space on the inner side of the kidney that collects urine. The ureter is a narrow muscular tube that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder by peristalsis. It is not the urethra, which carries urine from the bladder out of the body.

questions.prompt: Describe the path of urine from where it forms in the kidney to where it leaves the body.
questions.model: Urine forms continuously in the nephrons and drains from the collecting ducts into the renal pelvis. Peristalsis in the ureter carries it to the bladder in small spurts. As the bladder fills its wall stretches, and stretch receptors send nerve impulses that give the urge to urinate. To urinate, the muscular wall of the bladder contracts and the sphincters relax, the outer one under voluntary control. Urine leaves the body through the urethra.

questions.prompt: Relate the structure of the urinary system to its function of filtering and removing waste.
questions.model: The renal artery branches directly from the aorta, so blood arrives at high pressure, which drives filtration. The cortex is full of capillary knots (glomeruli) and Bowman's capsules, so it is the site of filtration. Each kidney has about one million nephrons, giving a huge filtering surface. Reabsorption happens in the cortex (coiled tubules) and in the medulla (loops of Henle and collecting ducts), returning glucose, amino acids, most salts and most water to the blood. The renal pelvis is a funnel that collects urine. The muscular ureters move urine to the bladder by peristalsis. The elastic bladder with its sphincters stores urine and allows controlled release, and the urethra is the exit. The fat layer protects each kidney from physical damage.
